questions.stem: In an unresponsive patient, what is the most common cause of anatomic airway obstruction?
questions.why: With decreased LOC, the tongue relaxes and falls against the posterior pharynx — the classic cause of anatomic obstruction, managed with suction, OPA/NPA, and positioning.

options.t: Muscular bronchospasm occurring in the lower airway
options.why: Bronchospasm is a lower-airway problem, not an anatomic upper obstruction.

options.t: The tongue falling back against the posterior pharynx
A foreign body lodged somewhere further down the airway
options.why: A foreign body is a distinct, less common cause than the tongue.

options.t: Swelling of the larynx from an active infection
options.why: Laryngeal edema is an infectious cause, not the top general cause.

questions.stem: According to Poiseuille's law, what happens to airway resistance as a tube's diameter decreases?
questions.why: Poiseuille's law explains why even mild airway swelling from infection can cause a large jump in resistance to airflow.

options.t: Airflow speeds up with no resistance penalty
options.why: A narrower tube does not increase flow for free; resistance rises.

options.t: Resistance decreases as diameter decreases
options.why: This reverses the actual relationship described.

options.t: Resistance stays the same regardless of diameter
options.why: Diameter has a dramatic effect on resistance in this relationship — it does not stay constant.

options.t: Resistance to flow increases sharply

questions.stem: What is the classic symptom triad of croup?
questions.why: Croup, an upper airway inflammation, classically presents with stridor, hoarseness, and a barking cough.

options.t: Rhonchi, coughing up blood, and pain worse on breathing
options.why: Rhonchi and hemoptysis are not the croup triad.

options.t: Crackling rales, fast breathing, and sharp chest pain
options.why: Rales and chest pain suggest a different pulmonary process.

options.t: Wheezing, a fever, and a cough that produces sputum
options.why: Wheezing and productive cough point toward a lower airway process, not croup.

options.t: Stridor, a hoarse voice, and a distinctive barking cough

questions.stem: Why doesn't the trachea swell shut the way soft tissue can?
questions.why: The tracheal cartilage rings provide rigid structural support, which is why the trachea itself resists the kind of soft-tissue swelling seen higher in the airway.

options.t: Infection-driven swelling simply cannot reach that low
options.why: Swelling absolutely can extend toward and involve the trachea in severe cases.

options.t: Rigid cartilage rings give the trachea structural support
It has no mucosal lining at all that's even capable of swelling shut
options.why: The trachea does have mucosa and can be affected by inflammation — the key protection is structural.

options.t: It sits entirely outside the reach of the immune system
options.why: The trachea is very much within reach of the immune and inflammatory response.

questions.stem: For a croup patient who is alert and moving good air, what is the recommended approach?
questions.why: If the patient is alert and moving good air, minimal intervention and avoiding agitation is the priority — crying and struggling can worsen airway swelling and increase oxygen demand.

options.t: Give high-dose IM epinephrine before assessing anything
options.why: Reaching straight for IM epi before assessing severity skips the actual first step.

options.t: Minimize interventions and avoid agitating the child further
Perform aggressive suctioning no matter the discomfort caused
options.why: Aggressive unnecessary suctioning risks agitating and worsening the child's status.

options.t: Attempt to intubate right away to secure the airway
options.why: Intubation is reserved for a deteriorating airway, not a stable one moving good air.

questions.stem: What acid-base disturbance results from hypoventilation?
questions.why: CO2 accumulates in the blood and forms carbonic acid, dropping pH — respiratory acidosis that can progress toward metabolic acidosis if uncorrected.

options.t: Respiratory acidosis that the kidneys fully correct within minutes
options.why: Renal compensation works over hours to days, not minutes — the pH stays low in the meantime.

options.t: Respiratory alkalosis develops instead, with no acid buildup
options.why: Alkalosis is the hyperventilation pattern, the opposite problem.

options.t: Metabolic alkalosis occurs, with no respiratory component involved
options.why: Metabolic alkalosis is unrelated to a ventilation-rate problem like this.

options.t: Respiratory acidosis, which can progress toward metabolic acidosis

questions.stem: What is the management goal for a hypoventilating patient?
questions.why: The fix for hypoventilation is increasing effective ventilation — BVM assistance or high-flow oxygen — to blow off the accumulating CO2.

options.t: Withholding oxygen entirely and simply waiting on lab results before acting
options.why: Oxygen shouldn't be withheld pending labs in an acute hypoventilation situation.

options.t: Increase respiratory effort using BVM assistance or high-flow oxygen
Sedate the patient to blunt their own respiratory drive
options.why: Sedation would suppress respiratory drive further, working against the goal.

options.t: Encourage the patient to breathe more slowly and shallowly
options.why: Slower, shallower breathing would worsen a hypoventilating patient's CO2 retention.

questions.stem: What acid-base change does hyperventilation cause?
questions.why: Hyperventilation blows off too much CO2, raising pH into respiratory alkalosis — which can cause numbness, tingling, and carpopedal spasms.

options.t: This produces a primary metabolic acidosis, not a respiratory one
options.why: Hyperventilation is a respiratory, not primary metabolic, disturbance.

options.t: Respiratory acidosis develops instead, dropping the pH
options.why: Acidosis is the hypoventilation pattern, the opposite direction.

options.t: Respiratory alkalosis that also drives serum potassium upward
options.why: Alkalosis pushes potassium into the cells, so serum potassium falls rather than rises.

options.t: Respiratory alkalosis develops, and blood pH climbs upward

questions.stem: Why might rebreathing exhaled air be dangerous for a hyperventilating patient?
questions.why: If hyperventilation is compensating for a true metabolic acidosis, rebreathing exhaled CO2 can mask or worsen that underlying problem — a classic reason paper-bag rebreathing is discouraged.

options.t: It converts the respiratory alkalosis into a metabolic alkalosis
options.why: Rebreathing raises CO2, which moves pH back toward acid — it cannot create a metabolic alkalosis.

options.t: The tingling and carpopedal spasm return the moment the bag comes off
options.why: Symptom rebound is not the hazard — the hazard is masking a metabolic acidosis the breathing was compensating for.

options.t: It may be compensating for a low pH, and rebreathing hides that
CO2 climbs faster than the respiratory center can adjust the rate
options.why: The respiratory center keeps responding normally; the danger is what the hyperventilation was compensating for.

questions.stem: How does heart failure create pulmonary consequences?
questions.why: Heart failure changes fluid balance and the pressures the right and left sides of the heart pump against, which backs up into the pulmonary circulation.

options.t: A failing myocardium consumes so much oxygen the alveoli are starved
options.why: Myocardial oxygen demand does not strip the alveoli — the pulmonary problem is backward pressure and fluid.

options.t: Inflammatory mediators from the failing heart scar the alveoli
options.why: Heart failure backs fluid up under pressure; it does not injure the lung by an inflammatory scarring mechanism.

options.t: Fluid-balance shifts change the pressures each side of the heart pumps against
Damage occurs through direct electrical injury to alveolar tissue
options.why: The pulmonary connection runs through pressure and fluid balance, not an electrical mechanism.

questions.stem: What mechanism actually brings air into the lungs during normal breathing?
questions.why: Normal breathing is driven by muscular control creating negative intrathoracic pressure, which draws air in — the opposite of positive-pressure ventilation.

options.t: Muscular effort creates negative pressure inside the chest cavity
Air is pushed in by positive pressure generated from outside the body
options.why: Positive pressure describes artificial ventilation (BVM), not normal spontaneous breathing.

options.t: The heart itself generates a suction effect that draws air inward
options.why: The heart does not generate the pressure gradient for ventilation.

options.t: Air moves in through passive diffusion with no muscle involvement
options.why: Muscular effort is required to generate the pressure gradient that draws air in.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'adventitious breath sounds'?
questions.why: Adventitious sounds — wheezes, rales, rhonchi, stridor — are extra sounds superimposed on the normal breath sounds, signaling pathology.

options.t: A complete absence of any breath sounds whatsoever on exam
options.why: Absent breath sounds is a distinct, separate finding from adventitious sounds.

options.t: Extra sounds layered on top of the normal breath sounds
Findings that indicate a completely normal, healthy lung exam
options.why: Adventitious sounds by definition indicate an abnormal finding, not a normal exam.

options.t: Sounds that are only assessed during an active cardiac arrest
options.why: Adventitious sounds are a general assessment category, not limited to codes.

questions.stem: What does grunting during respiration suggest?
questions.why: Grunting happens when a patient closes their glottis against exhalation, generating their own PEEP to keep alveoli open — a sign of significant respiratory distress.

options.t: The patient is generating their own intrinsic PEEP by grunting
A sign of bradycardia caused by strong vagal nerve stimulation
options.why: Grunting is a respiratory finding, not a description of a cardiac vagal response.

options.t: A benign sound that needs no further evaluation or concern
options.why: Grunting is a significant respiratory distress finding, not benign.

options.t: The airway is completely obstructed with zero air movement at all
options.why: Complete obstruction would not typically produce a grunting sound — that's closer to silence.

questions.stem: What are the two components driving airway narrowing in an asthma attack?
questions.why: Asthma involves both bronchospasm (muscle constriction of the bronchi, treated with a nebulized bronchodilator) and bronchial edema (swelling, treated with a corticosteroid).

options.t: Bronchospasm alone, with no inflammatory component involved at all
options.why: Edema is a real, separate contributor beyond spasm alone.

options.t: An underlying pulmonary embolism combined with bronchospasm
options.why: Pulmonary embolism is an unrelated, separate pathology.

options.t: Mucus plugging with collapse of the alveoli behind the plugs
options.why: Mucus does contribute, but the two components that define the asthma attack are bronchospasm and bronchial edema.

options.t: Bronchospasm from muscle constriction and bronchial edema from swelling

questions.stem: Bronchospasm and bronchial edema in asthma are treated differently. Why?
questions.why: A nebulized bronchodilator (albuterol) treats the muscular bronchospasm, while a corticosteroid (like Atrovent in this context) addresses the inflammatory edema.

options.t: A bronchodilator eases spasm but a steroid is needed for the swelling
Both problems resolve fully with a bronchodilator used alone
options.why: A bronchodilator alone does not resolve the edema component.

options.t: A steroid treats the spasm while a bronchodilator treats the swelling
options.why: This swaps the two mechanisms — corticosteroids target the edema, not the spasm.

options.t: Both respond to a corticosteroid, so the bronchodilator is optional
options.why: A steroid does nothing for acute bronchospasm — the bronchodilator is the time-critical drug, not the optional one.

questions.stem: What is status asthmaticus?
questions.why: Status asthmaticus is a severe, prolonged asthma attack that does not respond to standard bronchodilator therapy — a true emergency.

options.t: A mild attack that resolves completely on its own without help
options.why: A mild, self-resolving attack is the opposite of status asthmaticus.

options.t: An asthma attack that fails to respond to standard treatment
An asthma presentation seen only in the pediatric population
options.why: Status asthmaticus is not defined by, or limited to, a pediatric population.

options.t: A chronic baseline diagnosis with no acute component to it
options.why: This describes a chronic baseline state, not the acute refractory attack being defined.

questions.stem: What assessment finding in a severe asthma attack is especially concerning?
questions.why: Inaudible breath sounds mean the patient is moving so little air that wheezing can't even be generated — a hallmark of a severe, exhausting asthma attack, along with accessory muscle use and acidosis.

options.t: A patient reporting only mild, tolerable chest tightness
options.why: Mild chest tightness alone doesn't describe the severe end of the spectrum.

options.t: A normal respiratory rate paired with clear lung sounds
options.why: Normal rate and clear sounds would not indicate a severe attack at all.

options.t: Loud wheezing that can be heard clearly across the whole chest
options.why: Loud wheezing means air is still moving — inaudible sounds are the ominous sign of a nearly silent chest.

options.t: Inaudible breath sounds from very little air actually moving

questions.stem: What underlies emphysema at the alveolar level?
questions.why: Emphysema involves destroyed alveolar walls and lost surfactant, producing hyperinflation (barrel chest) and reduced surface area for gas exchange.

options.t: Alveoli are damaged and destroyed, and surfactant is lost
Excess mucus builds up while alveoli stay structurally normal
options.why: That description better fits chronic bronchitis, a different COPD component.

options.t: Fluid fills alveoli that otherwise remain normally structured
options.why: Fluid-filled but otherwise normal alveoli describes something closer to pulmonary edema.

options.t: Muscular bronchospasm occurs with no structural lung change
options.why: Emphysema is defined by actual structural alveolar destruction, not spasm alone.

questions.stem: Why must supplemental oxygen be given cautiously to a patient with emphysema who is on a hypoxic drive?
questions.why: In chronic CO2 retainers, the stimulus to breathe can shift from rising CO2 to falling O2 — giving too much oxygen can blunt that drive, so it's titrated carefully rather than withheld.

options.t: Oxygen thickens their secretions and plugs the small airways
options.why: Oxygen does not plug airways — the caution is that raising PaO2 can blunt a drive that depends on low oxygen.

options.t: Their drive comes from low oxygen instead of rising CO2 levels
Their chemoreceptors track pH alone, so oxygen level is irrelevant
options.why: Central chemoreceptors do track pH, but in a chronic retainer it is the peripheral receptors sensing low oxygen that carry the drive.

options.t: Oxygen constricts the pulmonary vessels and strains the right heart
options.why: Oxygen dilates pulmonary vessels — hypoxia is what causes pulmonary vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: What defines chronic bronchitis?
questions.why: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by excessive mucus production in the bronchial tree and a chronic productive cough.

options.t: A sudden bout of bronchospasm with no prior chronic history
options.why: Chronic bronchitis is defined by its chronic, ongoing nature, not an acute isolated event.

options.t: A restrictive pattern caused by a stiffened chest wall
options.why: Chronic bronchitis is an obstructive, not restrictive, process.

options.t: Excess mucus production in the bronchial tree with a chronic cough
Alveolar walls destroyed over time, leaving the chest overinflated and barrel-shaped
options.why: Destroyed alveoli and hyperinflation describe emphysema, a different COPD component.

questions.stem: What organisms can cause pulmonary infections like pneumonia?
questions.why: Pulmonary infections can be caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or protozoa — all producing airway swelling, mucus, and pus that narrow the airway per Poiseuille's law.

options.t: Only viruses cause it, since bacteria can't infect the lungs
options.why: Bacterial pneumonia is common and well documented — viruses aren't the sole cause.

options.t: Bacteria are the only organism capable of causing this infection
options.why: Bacteria are one of several causative categories, not the only one.

options.t: Fungal organisms alone, limited to immunocompromised patients
options.why: Fungal causes are one category among several, not exclusive to any one group.

options.t: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa can all cause infection

questions.stem: Which patient population carries an increased risk of pneumonia?
questions.why: Pneumonia risk climbs with advanced age, chronic illness, smoking and immunosuppression — each one impairs either mucociliary clearance or the immune response that would otherwise clear the organism.

options.t: Patients recovering at home from an uncomplicated outpatient procedure
options.why: A short outpatient recovery is not the risk profile — age, chronic illness, immunosuppression and smoking are.

options.t: Adults with seasonal allergies and well-controlled asthma
options.why: Controlled reactive airway disease on its own does not carry the elevated pneumonia risk that chronic illness and immunosuppression do.

options.t: Geriatric, chronically ill, immunocompromised patients, and smokers
Young and otherwise healthy adults with no significant history
options.why: A young, healthy adult clears aspirated organisms well; risk climbs with age, chronic disease, immunosuppression and smoking.

questions.stem: What lung sounds are especially associated with pneumonia, and where?
questions.why: Pneumonia commonly produces crackles or rhonchi, especially heard in the lung bases where infected, fluid-filled tissue tends to settle.

options.t: Crackles or rhonchi, heard especially down in the lung bases
Complete silence heard across both lung fields on exam
options.why: Pneumonia doesn't typically present as silent lungs — sounds are usually present, just abnormal.

options.t: Stridor, heard especially at the level of the trachea itself
options.why: Stridor is an upper-airway finding, not the classic pneumonia sound.

options.t: A pleural friction rub alone, with nothing else present
options.why: A friction rub is a different, distinct finding, not the hallmark pneumonia sound described.

questions.stem: What is atelectasis?
questions.why: Atelectasis is alveolar collapse from obstruction, external pressure, smoke, or toxin damage — and it can become a starting point for pneumonia.

options.t: Alveolar walls permanently destroyed, as seen in emphysema
options.why: Atelectasis is collapse, which is a different structural problem than the permanent destruction seen in emphysema.

options.t: Air trapped between the pleural layers, compressing the lung
options.why: That is a pneumothorax. Atelectasis is collapse of the alveoli themselves, not air in the pleural space.

options.t: A widespread bronchospasm affecting the lower airway broadly
options.why: Bronchospasm narrows airways by constricting smooth muscle; atelectasis is the alveoli themselves collapsing.

options.t: Alveoli collapsed by obstruction or outside pressure, filled with fluid

questions.stem: How does water solubility affect where a toxic gas causes damage?
questions.why: Highly water-soluble gases react quickly with moist mucus membranes, causing upper airway irritation and swelling; less soluble gases penetrate deeper into the lower airway, causing damage over time.

options.t: Solubility sets how fast the gas is exhaled again, not where it lands
options.why: Solubility governs where the gas reacts with airway moisture — a highly soluble gas is consumed in the upper airway before it can travel deeper.

options.t: Poorly soluble gases cause immediate upper-airway swelling on contact
options.why: That is the highly soluble pattern. Poorly soluble gases slip past the upper airway and injure the lower airway over hours.

options.t: Solubility only matters for gases that are heavier than air
options.why: Vapor density decides where a gas collects in a space; solubility decides where in the airway it reacts.

options.t: They react with moist mucus membranes, swelling the upper airway

questions.stem: What is the first management priority for toxic gas inhalation?
questions.why: Stopping ongoing exposure by removing the patient from the gas source is the priority, before treating the resulting respiratory effects.

options.t: Give nebulized albuterol right away before anything else
options.why: Bronchodilator treatment matters, but removing ongoing exposure comes first.

options.t: Get the patient away from the source of the toxic gas
Perform a 12-lead ECG before addressing anything else
options.why: A 12-lead is not the first priority in an acute toxic exposure scenario.

options.t: Start chest compressions no matter the patient's pulse status
options.why: Compressions are only indicated for a pulseless patient, not as the universal first step.

questions.stem: What clinical picture does toxic inhalation commonly produce?
questions.why: Toxic inhalation classically produces airway irritation and can progress to pulmonary edema, managed by removing the patient from the gas and giving 100% oxygen with assisted ventilation as needed.

options.t: Isolated abdominal pain with no respiratory findings at all
options.why: Abdominal pain alone does not describe the primary picture of an inhalation injury.

options.t: A slowed heart rate that shows up with no other clinical findings present
options.why: Toxic inhalation is a respiratory event with respiratory findings, not simply a heart-rate change.

options.t: Improved oxygenation as a direct result of the gas itself
options.why: Toxic gases impair, not improve, oxygenation.

options.t: Irritation of the airway that can progress to pulmonary edema

questions.stem: What is a pneumothorax?
questions.why: A pneumothorax is air trapped between the visceral and parietal pleura, and weak spots (blebs) on the lung can predispose a person to one.

options.t: Air collects in the space between the visceral and parietal pleura
Pus fills up the bronchial tree in this presentation
options.why: Pus in the bronchial tree points toward an infectious process, not a pneumothorax.

options.t: Blood collects directly within the alveoli themselves
options.why: Blood within the alveoli is not the definition of a pneumothorax.

options.t: Fluid collects in the space between the visceral and parietal pleura
options.why: Fluid between the pleura describes a pleural effusion, a different entity.

questions.stem: What assessment findings suggest a simple pneumothorax?
questions.why: A pneumothorax classically presents with sharp pain after coughing, worsening dyspnea over minutes to hours, and absent or diminished lung sounds with unilateral chest movement.

options.t: Symmetric chest rise with clear lung sounds on both sides
options.why: Symmetric, clear findings would argue against a pneumothorax, not for one.

options.t: Sharp pain after coughing with absent or diminished sounds one side
Wheezing on both sides along with a productive, wet cough
options.why: Bilateral wheezing with productive cough points toward an infectious/obstructive process, not a pneumothorax.

options.t: A gradual onset of dyspnea over several long weeks rather than hours
options.why: The classic presentation is acute, not a gradual multi-week course.

questions.stem: When is chest decompression indicated for a pneumothorax?
questions.why: Decompression is reserved for those with absent lung sounds — the more severe tension-type presentation — while simple pneumothorax gets oxygen and monitoring.

options.t: When lung sounds are absent, matching a tension-type picture
When the trachea has deviated away from the affected side
options.why: Tracheal deviation is a late and unreliable sign — absent lung sounds with the tension picture is what drives the decision.

options.t: Once a chest x-ray has confirmed the pneumothorax
options.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated before imaging — waiting for a film costs the patient.

options.t: For any patient with diminished sounds and pleuritic chest pain
options.why: Diminished sounds with chest pain describes a simple pneumothorax, which gets oxygen and monitoring rather than a needle.

questions.stem: What is a pleural effusion?
questions.why: A pleural effusion is a blister-like collection of fluid between the pleura that can be caused by infection, tumor, or trauma (blood), and pushes the lung out of its normal position.

options.t: Air collects between the pleura, pushing the lung out of place
options.why: Air between the pleura describes a pneumothorax, the opposite fluid-type problem.

options.t: A collapse of alveoli caused by pressure applied from somewhere outside
options.why: Alveolar collapse describes atelectasis, a distinct entity.

options.t: Inflammation limited entirely to the bronchial tree itself
options.why: Pleural effusion is a pleural-space problem, not confined to the bronchial tree.

options.t: Fluid collects between the pleura and pushes the lung out of place

questions.stem: What positioning consideration matters for a pleural effusion patient?
questions.why: Pleural fluid moves with gravity, so position changes how much lung it compresses. Sitting the patient up — Fowler's position — drops the fluid to the base and frees the upper lung fields.

options.t: Trendelenburg shifts the effusion off the bases and improves gas exchange
options.why: Head-down positioning pushes the abdominal contents into the diaphragm and increases the work of breathing.

options.t: Lay the patient flat on the unaffected side to protect the good lung
options.why: Lying flat gives up the gravity advantage — an effusion patient usually breathes best sitting upright.

options.t: Position genuinely affects how comfortably the patient can breathe
Keep the patient supine so the fluid spreads out evenly
options.why: Spreading the fluid across the lung field increases the surface it compresses; upright lets it pool at the base.

questions.stem: What can cause a pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: A PE can come from a blood clot, a fat embolism after a fracture, amniotic fluid embolism, or an air embolism — all obstructing pulmonary circulation.

options.t: Chronic bronchospasm building up gradually over time
options.why: Bronchospasm is a muscular airway problem, unrelated to vascular embolism.

options.t: A clot, a fat embolism from a fracture, amniotic fluid, or air
A bacterial infection settling into the pulmonary artery itself
options.why: Infection is not the mechanism behind embolic obstruction.

options.t: Only a blood clot can ever cause this — nothing else applies
options.why: Blood clot is the most common source, but not the only one described.

questions.stem: What is the classic presentation of a pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: Classic PE presents with sudden dyspnea and cyanosis that doesn't improve with oxygen, sharp chest pain, and low SpO2 paired with a low EtCO2.

options.t: Symptoms that fully resolve just by resting for a while
options.why: PE does not simply resolve with rest — it's an acute vascular emergency.

options.t: A slow, mild breathlessness building gradually over weeks
options.why: A slow, gradual onset is the opposite of the sudden classic PE presentation.

options.t: A slowed heart rate paired with a completely normal SpO2 and EtCO2
options.why: PE classically shows low SpO2 and low EtCO2, not normal values, and doesn't typically present as isolated bradycardia.

options.t: Sudden dyspnea and cyanosis that oxygen therapy doesn't fix

questions.stem: Why is a low EtCO2 seen in pulmonary embolism, despite adequate ventilation?
questions.why: In PE, venous blood carrying CO2 can't reach the alveoli because the embolism has obstructed pulmonary circulation — so even with normal ventilation, less CO2 shows up in exhaled air.

options.t: The clot itself consumes CO2 as blood passes around it
options.why: A clot does not metabolize CO2 — the reading falls because blood carrying CO2 never reaches ventilated alveoli.

options.t: Hyperventilation is clearing out every last trace of CO2 completely
options.why: While anxiety-driven hyperventilation can occur, the core low-EtCO2 mechanism here is the blocked perfusion itself.

options.t: Obstructed circulation keeps venous CO2 from reaching the alveoli
Bronchospasm distal to the clot traps CO2 down in the alveoli
options.why: Nothing is trapped — the CO2 never arrives, because perfusion to those alveoli is blocked.

questions.stem: What is a saddle embolus?
questions.why: A saddle embolus is a large clot sitting at the point where the pulmonary artery splits into the left and right branches — a severe, often catastrophic presentation.

options.t: A large clot sitting at the pulmonary artery's left-right split
A slow-growing chronic clot producing very few symptoms
options.why: A saddle embolus is typically an acute, large, symptomatic event, not a slow chronic process.

options.t: A small clot confined to one narrow peripheral lung segment
options.why: A small peripheral clot is the opposite scale of what defines a saddle embolus.

options.t: An embolus that lodges specifically within the coronary arteries instead
options.why: Coronary artery obstruction is a different vascular bed than the pulmonary one described.

questions.stem: Which patient population carries an increased risk for pulmonary embolism?
questions.why: Bedridden patients, those on birth control (BCP), and those who've had recent surgery carry an increased risk of clot formation and PE.

options.t: Only patients who happen to be under twenty years old
options.why: Age under 20 alone is not the risk factor described — immobility, birth control, and surgery are.

options.t: Patients who are bedridden, on birth control, or post-surgical
Patients with no history of immobility or any recent surgery
options.why: Immobility and recent surgery are specifically named as risk factors, not their absence.

options.t: Highly active patients who exercise daily with no other risks
options.why: Regular activity without other risk factors is not the highlighted at-risk group here.

questions.stem: What is the general oxygen saturation goal for supportive respiratory care?
questions.why: 94% is described as the usual goal for standard interventions like supplemental oxygen, alongside IV access, psychological support, and positioning.

options.t: 94 percent, the usual target for supportive oxygen therapy
80 percent, since going any higher risks real toxicity
options.why: 80% is frank hypoxemia — well below any acceptable target, and oxygen toxicity is not a prehospital concern.

options.t: 88 to 92 percent, the range used for chronic CO2 retainers
options.why: 88–92% is the COPD-specific target; the general supportive goal for everyone else is 94%.

options.t: 100 percent, accepted only as a fully complete saturation
options.why: Driving saturation to 100% buys nothing over 94% and carries its own hyperoxia risk.

questions.stem: What general steps help decrease work of breathing in a distressed patient?
questions.why: Sitting the patient upright, removing restrictive clothing, and avoiding exertion like walking are basic steps to reduce the work of breathing.

options.t: Sit the patient upright and remove any restrictive clothing
Lay the patient flat no matter their own position of comfort
options.why: Flat positioning regardless of comfort ignores the patient's own compensatory positioning.

options.t: Have the patient walk out to the ambulance to save some time
options.why: Walking increases oxygen demand in an already-distressed patient — the opposite of the goal.

options.t: Tighten any loose clothing to give the chest extra support
options.why: Tightening clothing would restrict breathing further, not ease it.

questions.stem: Bronchodilators are appropriate for bronchospasm, but should generally be avoided for which conditions?
questions.why: Bronchodilators target bronchospasm specifically; they're not indicated for pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or heart disease, where the underlying problem isn't muscular airway constriction.

options.t: Essentially any patient who happens to be wheezing on exam
options.why: Wheezing broadly can still reflect bronchospasm that responds to a bronchodilator — this isn't the excluded group.

options.t: A pediatric patient presenting with symptoms of croup
options.why: Croup management is a separate airway issue not centered on this bronchodilator caution.

options.t: Asthma attacks and acute exacerbations of COPD specifically
options.why: Asthma and COPD are the classic bronchodilator-appropriate conditions, not the ones to avoid it for.

options.t: Pneumonia, pulmonary edema, and underlying heart disease

questions.stem: What is the role of corticosteroids in respiratory emergencies?
questions.why: Corticosteroids work by stopping the immune response, reversing the inflammatory bronchial edema component of conditions like asthma.

options.t: Acting as the first-line treatment choice for a pneumothorax
options.why: Pneumothorax is a mechanical problem addressed by decompression, not a corticosteroid indication.

options.t: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle directly within seconds
options.why: Rapid smooth-muscle relaxation is the bronchodilator's job, not the corticosteroid's slower anti-inflammatory action.

options.t: Increasing mucus production as a form of airway protection
options.why: Corticosteroids work against inflammation, not by increasing mucus production.

options.t: Stopping the immune response to reverse the bronchial edema

questions.stem: When restoring fluid balance in a respiratory patient, what caution applies?
questions.why: Because edema often signals a fluid-distribution problem rather than a true fluid deficit, checking liver margins and starting conservatively (e.g., 250cc) avoids worsening overload in pulmonary patients.

options.t: Avoid overload — check liver margins and start conservatively
Give a full liter bolus first, then reassess the lung sounds
options.why: A full liter before reassessing can tip a pulmonary patient into overload — start near 250 cc and reassess as you go.

options.t: Match the fluid given to the patient's estimated urine output
options.why: Output matching is an inpatient calculation — prehospital care starts conservatively and watches for signs of overload.

options.t: IV fluids are withheld entirely for any respiratory complaint
options.why: Fluids aren't universally withheld — pulmonary patients are simply started conservatively, such as with 250cc.

questions.stem: How should ventilation be adjusted when using CPAP or BiPAP-style support versus a standard BVM?
questions.why: CPAP/BiPAP-style support and automated transport ventilators are described as using lower ventilation rates, smaller volumes, and lower pressure compared to standard BVM technique.

options.t: Lower rates, smaller volumes, and lower pressure than a BVM
The exact same settings used for a standard BVM in every case
options.why: Identical settings ignores the distinct pressure dynamics of these support modes.

options.t: No adjustment between these devices is ever needed at all
options.why: An adjustment is explicitly called for when using these different support modes.

options.t: The maximum possible rate and volume no matter the device
options.why: Maximum settings regardless of device risks overventilation and barotrauma.

questions.stem: What do PIP and PEEP refer to in the context of ventilatory support?
questions.why: PIP (peak inspiratory pressure) is the pressure needed to create chest rise and fall, while PEEP is the pressure maintained to keep alveoli open at the end of exhalation.

options.t: PIP creates chest rise; PEEP keeps the alveoli open at rest
PIP is a measure of oxygen concentration, not of pressure
options.why: PIP refers to a pressure value, not an oxygen concentration.

options.t: PIP is a diagnostic test, and PEEP is a class of medication
options.why: Neither term describes a diagnostic test or medication in this context.

options.t: Both terms describe the exact same single pressure value
options.why: PIP and PEEP are distinct pressures measured at different points in the breath cycle.

questions.stem: A post-surgical patient has sudden dyspnea, sharp chest pain, clear bilateral breath sounds, SpO2 of 86%, and EtCO2 of 24. Cyanosis does not improve on high-flow oxygen. What fits best?
questions.why: Clear lung sounds with profound hypoxia, a low EtCO2, and cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen point to obstructed pulmonary circulation — recent surgery is a major PE risk factor.

options.t: Aspiration pneumonia
options.why: Aspiration pneumonia develops with adventitious sounds and a slower course.

options.t: Pulmonary embolism
Acute asthma exacerbation
options.why: Asthma produces wheezing and airway narrowing, not clear bilateral sounds.

options.t: Simple pneumothorax
options.why: A pneumothorax typically gives unilateral diminished or absent sounds.

questions.stem: An asthma patient who was loudly wheezing becomes quiet, with barely audible breath sounds and rising exhaustion. How should this change be interpreted?
questions.why: Wheezing requires moving air. A silent chest in a tiring asthmatic signals severe obstruction and impending respiratory failure, not improvement.

options.t: Unchanged — wheeze intensity reflects airway caliber, not airflow
options.why: A wheeze needs turbulent airflow to exist at all. When too little air moves, the wheeze disappears even though the airway is tighter than before.

options.t: Improving — the patient is finally able to rest
options.why: Exhaustion with a silent chest is deterioration, not restful improvement.

options.t: Worsening — too little air is moving to wheeze
Improving — the bronchospasm has clearly resolved
options.why: Treating a quiet chest as resolution is the classic and dangerous misread here.

questions.stem: A long-standing COPD patient on a hypoxic drive is placed on high-flow oxygen and becomes progressively sleepier with a rising EtCO2. What happened?
questions.why: In chronic CO2 retainers the drive to breathe can shift to low O2. Over-oxygenating removes that stimulus, so ventilation falls, CO2 climbs, and the patient becomes somnolent.

options.t: The oxygen caused immediate alveolar damage
options.why: Oxygen does not damage alveoli over a few minutes of prehospital use.

options.t: They are having an allergic reaction to oxygen
options.why: Oxygen is not an allergen and does not provoke that kind of reaction.

options.t: They developed an acute pulmonary embolism
options.why: A PE would not be caused by simply applying oxygen to this patient.

options.t: Their hypoxic respiratory stimulus was blunted

questions.stem: Why does a small amount of airway swelling cause far more distress in a toddler than the same swelling would in an adult?
questions.why: Poiseuille's law: resistance rises sharply as diameter shrinks. Because a child's airway starts far smaller, equal swelling consumes a much larger share of the lumen.

options.t: Pediatric alveoli are unable to exchange gas normally
options.why: Alveolar gas exchange itself is not what edema in the upper airway impairs.

options.t: Children have a fundamentally different lung structure
options.why: Pediatric anatomy differs in scale and proportion, not in fundamental structure.

options.t: Toddlers cannot generate any effective cough at all
options.why: Children can and do cough, which is not the mechanism at work here.

options.t: Resistance climbs steeply as tube diameter narrows

questions.stem: A patient has sharp pain after a coughing fit, worsening dyspnea over an hour, and absent breath sounds on the right with unilateral chest movement. What is the most likely problem?
questions.why: Sudden onset after coughing, progressive dyspnea, and unilateral absent sounds with asymmetric chest movement is the classic pneumothorax pattern.

options.t: Right-sided pleural effusion
options.why: An effusion builds more gradually and does not usually follow a sudden cough.

options.t: Right lower lobe pneumonia
options.why: Pneumonia presents with crackles or rhonchi rather than absent sounds.

options.t: Acute pulmonary edema
options.why: Pulmonary edema produces bilateral crackles, not a unilateral silent side.

options.t: Pneumothorax on the right side
